A.explanation: Two springs in series give $k/2$, in parallel with the third spring gives $k/2 + k = 1.5k$, which is less stiff than three in parallel.

B.explanation: Three springs in parallel share the load and have the same extension, so $k_{total} = k + k + k = 3k$, the largest value.

C.explanation: Two springs in parallel give $2k$, in series with the third spring gives $1/k_{total} = 1/2k + 1/k$, so $k_{total} = 2k/3$.

D.explanation: Three springs in series all carry the same force with triple the extension, so $k_{total} = k/3$, the smallest value.

hints: Look at each diagram and decide which springs must stretch by the same amount and which must carry the same force.
Recall that springs in parallel add directly as $k_{total} = k_1 + k_2 + ...$ while springs in series add reciprocally as $1/k_{total} = 1/k_1 + 1/k_2 + ...$.
Compare the stiffness of three springs all sharing the extension against any arrangement where two or three springs are end-to-end in series.
walkthrough: Let each identical spring have constant $k$. Springs side-by-side between the same bars are in parallel and have equal extension. Springs end-to-end are in series and carry equal force.
For parallel springs, the forces add, so $k_{total} = sum k$. For series springs, the extensions add, so $1/k_{total} = sum 1/k$.
In arrangement B all three springs are connected between the same two bars, so all three are in parallel: $k_{total} = k + k + k = 3k$.
In the other arrangements series combinations reduce the stiffness: A gives $k/2 + k = 1.5k$, C gives a $2k$ pair in series with $k$ to give $2k/3$, and D gives three in series to give $k/3$.
Since $3k$ is greater than $1.5k$, $2k/3$ and $k/3$, the all-parallel arrangement is stiffest. This is option B.
